blocks.text: We have learnt that a charge experiences an electrostatic force in the presence of other charges. Let us consider a positively charged object O. If we place a small charge +q at point A, it will experience an electrostatic force F due to the charged body O; thus an electric field is said to exist at point A. Coulomb's law suggests that the field gets stronger as the point A gets closer to O (Fig. 9.3). The strength of the field at a position is known as its intensity at that point.

blocks.alt: A circle O filled with + signs (a positively charged body). A dashed line leads from O to point A, where a small orange charge +q sits; a red arrow F continues from A directly away from O.
blocks.caption: Figure 9.3 (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 9.3).

blocks.title: Electric field intensity
blocks.text: The electric intensity of the field, or simply the electric field, at any point is defined as the force experienced by a unit positive charge placed at that point. Electric intensity is a force per unit charge, so it is a vector quantity, usually denoted by E: E = F/q ... (9.8).

From Eq. 9.8 the unit of electric intensity is newton per coulomb (N C^-1). The direction of E is the same as that of F. The equation can also be written as F = qE ... (9.9). For a point charge q in free space, combining with Coulomb's law gives E = k q / r^2 at distance r.

blocks.title: Example 9.2
blocks.text: Two positive point charges q1 = 16.0 uC and q2 = 4.0 uC are 3.0 m apart (Fig. 9.4). Find the spot on the line joining them where the electric field is zero. Solution: between the charges the two fields are opposite, so E is zero at P where E1 = E2. Let P be d from q2: (1/(4 pi eps0)) q1/(3.0 - d)^2 = (1/(4 pi eps0)) q2/d^2, so 16.0 x 10^-6/(9.0 + d^2 - 6d) = 4.0 x 10^-6/d^2, giving d^2 + 2d - 3 = 0, d = +1 m or -3 m. The negative value lies to the right of both charges, where E1 and E2 have equal magnitudes but the same direction, so they do not cancel. Hence d = +1.0 m from q2.

blocks.alt: +q1 on the left and +q2 (point O) on the right, joined by a line; a dashed double arrow below marks 3.0 m. The point P lies between them nearer q2; a double arrow above marks the distance d from P to q2.
blocks.caption: Figure 9.4 (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 9.4).

blocks.title: Example 9.3
blocks.text: A proton experiences an electrostatic force equal to its weight at a particular point in an electric field. What is the field intensity there? (mass of proton = 1.67 x 10^-27 kg, e = 1.6 x 10^-19 C.) Solution: E = F/q = mg/e = (1.67 x 10^-27 kg x 9.8 m s^-2)/(1.6 x 10^-19 C) = 1.0 x 10^-7 N C^-1.

A visual representation of the electric field can be obtained in terms of electric field lines, an idea proposed by Michael Faraday. Electric field lines can be considered as a visual map used to represent the direction and strength of an electric field around a charged object; as they give information about the electric force exerted on a charged object, these lines are commonly called electric lines of force. To introduce them, we place positive test charges +q0 at equal distances from a positive charge +q (Fig. 9.5). Each test charge experiences a repulsive force, so the field created by +q is directed radially outward. Figure 9.6 shows the field lines near a negative charge -q: the lines are directed radially inward, because the force on a positive test charge is now attractive.

blocks.alt: (a) Eight small orange test charges +q0 on a dotted circle round a central charge +q; a magenta arrow points radially outward from each. (b) Straight field lines radiating from +q in all directions with arrowheads pointing outward.
blocks.caption: Figure 9.5: (a) A positive test charge +q0 placed anywhere near a positive point charge +q experiences a repulsive force directed radially outward; (b) the field lines are directed radially outward from +q (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 9.5).

blocks.alt: A blue charge -q with straight field lines coming in from all directions; the arrowheads point inward, towards -q.
blocks.caption: Figure 9.6: The electric field lines are directed radially inward towards a negative point charge -q (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 9.6).

blocks.text: Figures 9.5 and 9.6 are two-dimensional pictures; field lines in fact emerge from charges in three dimensions, and an infinite number of lines could be drawn. The field-line map also gives the strength of the field: the lines are closer to each other near the charges, where the field is strong, and spread out further away, showing a continuous decrease in field strength.

blocks.title: Field line density
blocks.text: The number of lines per unit area passing perpendicularly through it is proportional to the magnitude of the electric field.

The lines are curved for two identical separated charges. Figure 9.7 shows the pattern for two identical positive point charges of equal magnitude: the lines in the region between the two like charges seem to repel each other, and the middle region shows a zero-field spot or neutral zone; two identical negative charges behave in the same way. Figure 9.8 shows two opposite charges of equal magnitude: the lines start from the positive charge and end on the negative charge; the field at points such as 1, 2, 3 is the resultant of the fields of the two charges, and its direction is given by the tangent drawn to the field line at that point. Where the lines are parallel and equally spaced, the same number of lines pass per unit area and the field is uniform, as in the middle region between the plates of a parallel plate capacitor (Fig. 9.9).

blocks.alt: Two equal positive charges +q side by side. Field lines leave each charge in all directions and curve away from the other charge; between them the lines bend apart, leaving an empty zero-field spot midway.
blocks.caption: Figure 9.7: The electric field lines for two identical positive point charges (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 9.7).

blocks.alt: A positive charge +q (left) and a negative charge -q (right). Field lines leave +q, curve round and end on -q; outer lines leave the picture from +q and others come in from outside to -q. Points 1, 2 and 3 on three lines carry short red arrows along the tangent.
blocks.caption: Figure 9.8: The electric field lines of two opposite charges of equal magnitude (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 9.8).

blocks.alt: Two vertical plates, + on the left and - on the right. Between them parallel, evenly spaced field lines point from + to -. Near the top and bottom edges the lines bulge outward in curves; outside, lines leave the + plate to the left and come in to the - plate from the right.
blocks.caption: Figure 9.9: In the central region of a parallel plate capacitor, the electric field lines are parallel and evenly spaced, indicating that the electric field there has the same magnitude and direction at points (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 9.9).

items: Electric field lines originate from positive charges and end on negative charges.
The tangent to a field line at any point gives the direction of the electric field at that point.
The lines are closer where the field is strong and farther apart where the field is weak.
No two lines cross each other, because E has only one direction at any given point; if lines crossed, E would have more than one direction.

blocks.text: There is no electric field inside a conductor (Do You Know).
